options: O(n^2) for LinkedList due to get(i)
explanation: ArrayList.get(i) is O(1), but LinkedList.get(i) is O(n); repeated calls in a loop make it O(n^2) for LinkedList.
HashSet.contains() is O(1) on average; ArrayList.contains() is O(n); for large collections, B is much faster.
Arrays have excellent cache locality; sequential access is CPU-cache-friendly and very fast.
Integer.valueOf() caches values -128 to 127; reuses objects instead of creating new ones, saving memory.
Exception creation is expensive (stack trace generation); using exceptions for control flow is a performance anti-pattern.
For ArrayList, enhanced for-loop (A) uses iterator which is optimized; for-i loop (B) calls get(i) repeatedly.
Each ++ operation unboxes, increments, and boxes, creating new Integer objects repeatedly; use int primitive instead.

options: JIT compiles hot code to native, optimizes
explanation: JIT (Just-In-Time) compilation detects hot code paths and compiles them to native machine code with optimizations.
String += creates new String objects; 1000 iterations create 1000 intermediate strings (O(n^2) time complexity).
